note_claims.claim: The patient presented with a hypoglycaemic episode approximately three months ago after skipping lunch while gardening, characterized by sweating, shakiness, and confusion.
The patient's daughter (who has type 1 diabetes) found him confused and measured his capillary glucose at 2.8 mmol/L.
The patient recovered within 15 minutes after being treated with orange juice and biscuits.
The patient experiences occasional pre-meal wobbliness.
The patient is prescribed Metformin 1g twice daily.
The patient is prescribed Gliclazide 80 mg twice daily (morning and teatime).
The patient is prescribed Atorvastatin 20 mg and Ramipril 5 mg.
The patient's blood pressure is 138/84.
The patient's weight is 91 kg.
The patient has a callus under the right first metatarsal head.
The patient's HbA1c is 62 mmol/mol, which is an increase from the previous level of 58 mmol/mol.
The patient's eGFR is 52, which is stable.
The impression is Type 2 diabetes with recent hypoglycaemia on gliclazide and HbA1c above target.
The plan is to continue gliclazide 80 mg twice daily and start empagliflozin 10 mg once daily.
A podiatry referral is planned for the callus, and retinal screening is to be booked.
Safety netting includes checking blood glucose before driving and every two hours on long journeys.
The patient must not drive if their blood sugar is below 5 mmol/L.
The patient must keep fast-acting glucose in the car.
If a severe hypo occurs (e.g., needing help from someone else), the patient must stop driving and inform the DVLA if another severe hypo occurs within 12 months or any hypo while driving.
The patient should stop empagliflozin if they are vomiting, have diarrhoea, or are unable to eat and drink.

transcript_facts.fact: Clinician greeted Mr Elsworth-Mahmood.
Patient's daughter, Yasmin, requested the appointment due to an incident last week.
Relative greeted the clinician.
Patient experienced symptoms including being sweaty, shaky, and unable to think straight.
The patient stated the episode occurred on Tuesday because it was bin day and he had just put them out.
The patient had been in the garden all morning and skipped lunch.
Relative found the patient confused and identified it as a hypoglycaemia due to her own type 1 diabetes.
Relative gave the patient orange juice and biscuits.
The patient recovered within about fifteen minutes.
Relative used her meter and measured the capillary glucose at 2.8 mmol/L.
Patient reported feeling a bit wobbly before tea sometimes.
Patient drives to the shops and to his allotment.
Patient confirmed he was not driving that day.
Clinician checked medications and found the patient is on metformin, one gram twice a day.
Patient confirmed the Metformin dose.
Clinician checked medications and found the patient is on gliclazide, 80 milligrams twice a day.
Patient confirmed the Gliclazide dosing schedule (morning and teatime).
Clinician checked medications and found the patient is on Atorvastatin 20 milligrams and ramipril 5 milligrams.
Patient confirmed all listed medications.
Clinician asked about allergies.
Patient reported no known drug allergies.
Clinician asked about problems with feet, tingling, or numbness.
Patient reported his feet have been fine.
Relative reported having pins and needles in her hands at night, which she suspects is carpal tunnel.
Clinician suggested sticking with the patient today.
Patient denied having problems with his eyesight.
Patient mentioned his eye screening is due.
Clinician noted the patient's blood tests from last week showed an HbA1c of 62 mmol/mol, up from 58 mmol/mol.
Clinician noted the patient's kidney function (eGFR) is 52, which is about the same as before.
Patient asked if the results were bad.
Clinician noted that sugar control has drifted up a little, but the hypo worries him more.
Clinician checked the patient's feet and noted pulses were fine in both feet.
Clinician noted that sensation was normal in both feet.
Clinician noted there was a bit of hard skin and a callus under the ball of the patient's left foot, by the big toe.
Patient stated he has had the callus for ages.
Clinician noted the patient's blood pressure is 138 over 84.
Clinician noted the patient's weight is 91 kilos.
Clinician suggested reducing the gliclazide dose to 80 milligrams in the morning only and stopping the teatime dose.
Clinician suggested adding empagliflozin, 10 milligrams once a day.
Clinician advised stopping empagliflozin when unwell and not eating or drinking (e.g., with vomiting or diarrhoea).
Clinician advised the patient to check his blood sugar before driving and every two hours on long journeys.
Clinician advised not to drive if blood sugar is below five.
Clinician advised keeping some sugary snacks in the car.
Clinician stated that needing daughter's help counts as a severe hypo.
Clinician stated that if another severe hypo occurs within 12 months, or any hypo while driving, the patient must stop driving and tell the DVLA.
Relative offered to get glucose tablets.
Clinician planned to refer the patient to the podiatrist for the callus and book his eye screening.
Clinician scheduled a review in three months with a repeat HbA1c and kidney test.
